description: Two-panel composite of compression yield-stress versus temperature plots for Fe-26Al-based alloys. Both panels share identical axes: y = "Yield stress in compression [MPa]", 0 to 800 with gridlabel ticks every 100; x = "Temperature [°C]", 0 to 900 with ticks every 100. No numeric data labels are printed on any curve - only marker symbols. (a) contains four curves (legend: Fe-26Al, Fe-26Al-2Ti-1C, Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C, Fe-26Al-2V-1C, with square, diamond, circle and triangle-down markers). All four start high at room temperature (Fe-26Al above the 600 MPa gridline, the Ti/V alloys near the 450-550 MPa gridlines), soften to a minimum between the 200 and 400 °C gridlines, then rise to a local maximum near 500-560 °C just above the 400 MPa gridline, and fall steeply towards 800 °C, where the binary Fe-26Al drops to the 0-50 MPa range. (b) replots the binary Fe-26Al curve together with three Nb/Ta alloys (legend: Fe-26Al, Fe-26Al-2Nb-1C, Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C, Fe-26Al-2Ta-1C). The anomalous peak of the Nb/Ta alloys is displaced to lower temperature and higher stress, and Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C lies highest at every temperature. The figure demonstrates yield-stress anomalies in Fe-26Al alloys and carbide/Laves-phase strengthening.

observations.observation: Both panels plot 'Yield stress in compression [MPa]' (y, 0-800, ticks every 100) against 'Temperature [°C]' (x, 0-900, ticks every 100); no numeric values are printed on any data point, so values can only be read against gridlines.
Panel (a) legend entries are exactly: Fe-26Al (open square), Fe-26Al-2Ti-1C (open diamond), Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C (open circle), Fe-26Al-2V-1C (inverted open triangle).
Panel (b) legend entries are exactly: Fe-26Al (open square), Fe-26Al-2Nb-1C (open triangle), Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C (asterisk), Fe-26Al-2Ta-1C (plus).
In panel (a) every curve has a local minimum between the 200 and 400 °C gridlines and a local maximum ('anomalous' peak) between roughly 500 and 560 °C, reaching just above the 400 MPa gridline.

In panel (a) the binary Fe-26Al curve is the highest at room temperature (above the 600 MPa gridline, with a first data point near 640 MPa by gridline reading) but becomes the lowest curve above ~650 °C, ending near the 0-50 MPa level at 800 °C.
In panel (b) Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C lies above all other curves at all plotted temperatures, beginning near the 800 MPa gridline at room temperature and peaking just above the 600 MPa gridline near 500 °C.
In panel (b) the peaks of Fe-26Al-2Nb-1C and Fe-26Al-2Ta-1C occur at lower temperature and higher stress than the peak of the binary Fe-26Al alloy in the same panel.
The caption identifies the figure as the temperature dependencies of the yield stress in compression for Fe-26Al-based alloys.

The citing text states that the peak temperature is about 550 °C and the peak yield stress about 400 MPa for the Fe-26Al alloys with Ti and V (Fig. 6a), which agrees with the position of the maxima seen in panel (a).

The citing text states that the alloy Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C exhibits the most significant shift of the peak position (474 °C, 619 MPa) and has the highest yield stresses at all tested temperatures; the plotted peak in panel (b) appears near 500 °C just above the 600 MPa gridline, so the printed 474 °C / 619 MPa values cannot be confirmed from the pixels.

The citing text attributes the high strength of the Nb-containing alloy to strengthening by the Laves phase (Fe, Al)2Nb, and states that MC carbide precipitation strengthening is also effective and more resistant to coarsening than the Laves phase.
The citing text reports that elevated-temperature compression testing was performed up to 800 °C, consistent with the upper limit of the x-axis in both panels.

The citing text describes the companion Fe-15Al-based alloys (Fig. 5, not shown here) as showing a gradual monotonous decrease of yield stress with temperature, i.e. without the anomaly seen in the Fe-26Al-based alloys in this figure.

sample_hints: Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C (474 °C, 619 MPa peak, as stated in text)

subfigures.description: Yield stress in compression (0-800 MPa) versus temperature (0-900 °C) for four Fe-26Al-based alloys: Fe-26Al, Fe-26Al-2Ti-1C, Fe-26Al-4Ti-1C and Fe-26Al-2V-1C. All curves show a room-temperature maximum, a minimum near 300-400 °C, a yield-stress-anomaly peak near 500-550 °C at about the 400-420 MPa level, and a steep drop to 800 °C. Binary Fe-26Al is strongest at room temperature but weakest above ~600 °C.

Same axes as (a) for Fe-26Al, Fe-26Al-2Nb-1C, Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C and Fe-26Al-2Ta-1C. Fe-26Al-4Nb-1C is the highest curve over the whole range, starting near the 800 MPa gridline and peaking just above the 600 MPa gridline at ~500 °C; the Nb- and Ta-containing alloys peak at lower temperature and higher stress than the binary Fe-26Al alloy.
